title: Center Pivot Irrigation in Spinach Cultivation: Challenges and Practical Solutions
html:
Introduction to Trench Irrigation for Leafy Greens

Trench irrigation, also known as strip irrigation, is one of the most advanced methods of water resource management, with high efficiency in dense and sensitive crops such as Cilantro (herbaceous) is highly effective. Cilantro is a plant sensitive to water and salinity stress, with shallow and delicate root systems. Therefore, precise distribution of water and nutrients around the roots is considered key to success in this crop. In this section, we examine how to balance the high water needs of cilantro with water resource limitations. Leafy green plants like cilantro are highly sensitive to soil moisture stability due to their shallow roots. Severe moisture fluctuations can lead to stem cracking, reduced aromatic quality, and even total crop loss. Trench irrigation resolves this issue by creating a stable wet zone. Compared to conventional drip irrigation, this method provides more uniform coverage of the root zone. This allows the plant to complete growth and flowering stages without stress. Additionally, because the strip system delivers water flow continuously and at low pressure, the risk of physical damage to delicate roots is reduced. These characteristics have made strip irrigation the preferred option for many vegetable crops in arid and semi-arid regions. Farmers seeking to increase yield volume and reduce manual operation costs should focus on this technology. Of course, proper implementation of this system requires significant technical knowledge, which we will discuss later.

Why does Cilantro need Trench Irrigation?

  • Delicate root system: The root mass of choy (mustard greens) typically extends to a depth of 20 to 40 cm. Surface irrigation causes root washing and fungal diseases. In axillary irrigation, water is directed directly to the root zone, keeping the soil surface drier, which enhances resistance.
  • Salinity sensitivity: This crop is highly sensitive to surface soil salinity accumulation. Axillary irrigation can help maintain yield by creating a low-salinity root zone. Additionally, dissolved salts in groundwater across many regions of Iran pose a significant challenge that can only be managed using systems equipped with brine boilers.
  • Efficiency improvement: By using seed distribution and yield guidelines for similar crops yield variables can be optimized. Managing planting density and water dose has a direct relationship with the harvested leafy volume. Optimizing these two parameters increases profitability per square meter of land.

Main challenges in axillary irrigation of choy

Uniform water distribution along the entire length of a drip tape is not straightforward. Challenges can be categorized into three groups: technical, edaphological, and agronomic. Accurate identification of these obstacles is the first step toward overcoming them.

1. Clogging of drip emitters and drip tape channels

The use of groundwater with high salinity or inadequate treatment leads to salt precipitation and biofilm growth in drip emitters and drip tape slits. Clogging causes uneven water distribution, resulting in relative drought stress and reduced weight per dozen shaw seeds. To prevent this, the use of appropriate filters, such as screen or disc filters, and regular system flushing are essential. Additionally, using drip tape with high-quality tubing prevents the ingress of fine particles into the slits. In this regard, review Specifications of woven hoses and drip tape is critical to ensure the durability and resistance of the system to pressure and UV radiation. Periodic maintenance and visual inspections extend the useful life of the equipment.

2. Salinity and water EC management

If the Electrical Conductivity (EC) of the water used exceeds 1 dS/m, new shaw leaves will suffer damage without additional irrigation for salt flushing. The main challenge is that the plant requires frequent, low-volume irrigation to control salinity, which is not compatible with standard pivot systems designed for larger trees. Irrigation doses must be adjusted using salinity factors. Specifically, the water volume must be increased enough to remove excess salt from the root zone. Calculating this dose requires water and soil testing.

3. Soil Dynamics and Root Structure

Heavy, textured soils have low permeability. Under these conditions, trunk irrigation can rapidly saturate the root zone and cause relative alkalinization of the soil matrix. Prolonged saturation disrupts root aeration and suffocates the roots. For specific crops, study Climatic maps and regional conditions help align the irrigation type with local conditions. In clay soils, irrigation cycles should be longer with lower doses to ensure deep penetration. In sandy soils, the opposite applies. Understanding soil texture is a prerequisite for success in any crop.

Practical Solutions and Technical Adjustments

To overcome the challenges mentioned, the implementation of the following practical tips is recommended. These adjustments are based on successful experiences in vegetable farms.

  1. Adjusting Dripper Spacing: A 20 cm spacing is optimal for dense root systems. Ensure the dripper line is centered exactly in the row to achieve uniform wetting. Deviation of the line from the row creates heterogeneous dry and wet zones around the plant, which must be corrected by adjusting the pipe alignment.
  2. Irrigation Pattern Change: Instead of one heavy irrigation session, use multiple light applications. This helps promote young root development. Dividing the irrigation volume into several stages maintains soil moisture at an acceptable level. Avoid heavy water loads that cause soil erosion or waterlogging.
  3. Use of Elevated Tape Drip Line: For hard soils, using an elevated tape drip line can prevent soil erosion under the root zone and provide more controlled water flow. This method is also applicable for sloped soils. When rooting depth is limited, elevated tape lines reduce the risk of mechanical damage.

Agricultural Operations Map

A scheduled plan for planting and harvesting is crucial. Reviewing care points for plant maintenance and sowing can help determine critical irrigation periods. Additionally, soil temperature directly affects root activation. During hot months, plant transpiration rates increase, raising water demand. In cold months, growth slows, and irrigation doses should be reduced to prevent fungal diseases. Aligning the irrigation schedule with the plant’s biological calendar is key to efficiency.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

How many times a day should we irrigate the corn?

This depends on temperature and climate. In hot weather, 2 to 3 times per day with small doses is recommended. Total water application should be adjusted to match ET (evapotranspiration). There is a golden rule: monitor the plants for stress. If new leaves wilt, it means sufficient water has not reached them. Immediate system correction minimizes damage. Also, using soil moisture sensors turns this guesswork into precise measurement.

Can chemical fertilizer be applied through drip irrigation?

Yes, but only water-soluble fertilizers that are environmentally safe for the system. You must ensure the fertilizers are non-sediment forming. Fertigation through center pivot systems increases uptake efficiency. Do not use large amounts of acidic fertilizers, as they may damage the sprinklers. In this context, understanding the advantages and disadvantages of direct irrigation and comparing it with center pivot systems is useful. Point application of fertilizer in a center pivot system reduces waste.

What should we do if the drip line is damaged?

Welding or the use of specific repair compounds can resolve leaks. Never use glue or non-agricultural materials. Water leaks not only waste resources but also create overly wet spots that promote fungal growth. Quick repairs contribute to the health of the entire crop. Having spare parts for lines may not seem necessary, but in practice, it is vital.

What is the difference between tape drip lines and conventional drip emitters?

Tape drip lines are continuous strips that distribute water uniformly. Conventional drip emitters are discrete points. Tape drip lines are better suited for crops with dense rows, such as radishes. The uniform distribution from the tape ensures synchronized growth across the entire row. While conventional drip emitters may only irrigate the root zone center, tape drip lines cover the entire root zone surface. This characteristic is particularly important for vegetables with extensive root systems.

Conclusion

Radish pivot irrigation is a sensitive process requiring precise monitoring. The main challenges include managing salinity, preventing emitter clogging, and fine-tuning water distribution. By adhering to engineering and agronomic principles, farmers can achieve maximum yield with minimal water usage. Farmers can complete their planning by utilizing reliable resources such as similar crop yield guidesto supplement their strategies. Success in this process requires patience, precision, and continuous awareness of soil and plant conditions. Investing in a high-quality pivot irrigation system yields significant long-term economic returns. It is advisable to conduct a comprehensive audit of water sources and equipment before the planting season begins. Additionally, training staff on the correct operation of sprinklers and dosage adjustments is a fundamental pillar of effective management.
